## ARTICLE 16 — EVENTS OF DEFAULT

### 16.1 Events of Default

Each of the following shall constitute an "**Event of Default**" under this Mortgage and the other Loan Documents:

(a) **Payment.** Failure by Borrower to make any payment of principal, interest, the Yield Maintenance Premium, a late charge or any other amount due under the Loan Documents when due, subject to the cure period set forth in Section 16.2(a);

(b) **Covenant Default.** Breach by Borrower of any covenant, agreement or obligation contained in this Mortgage or in any other Loan Document (other than a breach described in any other clause of this Section 16.1), continuing beyond the applicable cure period set forth in Section 16.2(b);

(c) **Misrepresentation.** Any representation or warranty made by Borrower or Guarantor in any Loan Document, or in any certificate or report delivered in connection therewith, proving to be materially false, misleading or inaccurate in any material respect when made or deemed made;

(d) **Bankruptcy; Insolvency.** The filing by Borrower or Guarantor of a voluntary petition under the United States Bankruptcy Code or any state insolvency, receivership or reorganization law, the consent by Borrower or Guarantor to the appointment of a receiver, trustee or custodian for any substantial part of its property or assets, any assignment for the benefit of creditors by Borrower or Guarantor, the admission in writing by Borrower or Guarantor of its inability to pay its debts generally as they become due, or the filing of an involuntary petition against Borrower or Guarantor that is not dismissed within sixty (60) days, or the appointment of a receiver, trustee or custodian for any substantial part of the property or assets of Borrower or Guarantor that is not discharged within sixty (60) days;

(e) **Cross-Default.** A default by Borrower or Guarantor under any other indebtedness for borrowed money in an amount exceeding Two Hundred Fifty Thousand and No/100 Dollars ($250,000.00), individually or in the aggregate, which default is not cured within any applicable cure or grace period, or the acceleration of any such indebtedness;

(f) **Insurance.** Failure by Borrower to maintain any insurance required under Article 11 or to deliver the certificates and endorsements required by Section 11.6, subject to the cure period set forth in Section 16.2(d);

(g) **DSCR.** The DSCR being less than 1.25 to 1.00 as of two (2) consecutive DSCR Test Dates, without cure in accordance with Section 13.5;

(h) **Reserves.** Failure by Borrower to make any deposit into any Reserve Account when required, or failure to replenish the Tenant Improvement and Leasing Commission Reserve Account within thirty (30) days after Lender's written demand in accordance with Section 6.3, or failure to make any deposit into the Capital Replacement Reserve Account or the Tax and Insurance Escrow Account;

(i) **Single-Purpose Entity.** Breach of any covenant set forth in Article 14, including any failure to maintain an Independent Manager or any amendment to the Operating Agreement that eliminates or weakens any single-purpose entity, separateness or bankruptcy-remoteness provision;

(j) **Substantial Completion.** Failure by Borrower to achieve Substantial Completion of the renovation on or before the Substantial Completion Deadline, subject to Section 16.2(e);

(k) **Transfer Restrictions.** Any sale, transfer, encumbrance, pledge or other disposition of the Property or of any direct or indirect interest in Borrower in violation of Section 10.2, or any change of control of Borrower or of a Controlling Member without Lender's prior written consent;

(l) **Land Use Restriction; Environmental.** Any failure by Borrower to comply with the LUR or with any covenant set forth in Article 12, including without limitation any use of the ground floor of Lot 7 for residential purposes, any penetration, removal or compromise of the vapor barrier beneath the Bay 1 floor slab without SCDHEC approval and Lender consent, any failure to conduct or deliver the vapor barrier inspections required by Section 12.2(c), or any modification, termination or vacation of the LUR without Lender's consent;

(m) **Material Adverse Effect.** The occurrence of a Material Adverse Effect that, in Lender's reasonable judgment, materially impairs the ability of Borrower to perform its obligations under the Loan Documents or of Guarantor to perform its obligations under the Guaranty, the Completion Guaranty or the Payment Guaranty;

(n) **Guaranty.** A default by Guarantor under the Guaranty, the Completion Guaranty, the Payment Guaranty or the Environmental Indemnity, or any attempt by Guarantor to revoke, terminate, disavow or limit its liability thereunder;

(o) **Abandonment.** The abandonment of the Property, the cessation of operations at the Property for more than thirty (30) consecutive days (other than as a result of a casualty or condemnation being diligently restored), or the removal from the Property of a material portion of the Collateral;

(p) **Other Loan Documents.** The occurrence of any other event or condition that constitutes an Event of Default under any other Loan Document; or

(q) **Invalidity.** Any Loan Document ceasing to be in full force and effect, or any party thereto asserting that any Loan Document is not a valid and binding obligation of such party, or any lien granted under this Mortgage ceasing to be a valid first-priority lien on the Property (subject only to the Permitted Exceptions).

### 16.2 Notice and Cure Periods

The following cure periods shall apply to the Events of Default described in Section 16.1:

(a) **Payment Defaults.** Five (5) Business Days after the date on which payment was due.

(b) **Non-Monetary Defaults.** Thirty (30) calendar days after written notice from Lender to Borrower of the default; provided, however, that if the default is of a nature that it cannot reasonably be cured within thirty (30) calendar days and Borrower has commenced and is diligently pursuing the cure thereof, the cure period shall be extended for an additional period not to exceed sixty (60) calendar days (for a total cure period not to exceed ninety (90) calendar days). No such notice or cure period shall apply to any default that consists of a failure to pay money or to any Event of Default described in Section 16.2(c), (d) or (e).

(c) **Single-Purpose Entity, Transfer and Bankruptcy Defaults.** No cure period. Any breach of the covenants set forth in Article 14 or Section 10.2, and any event described in Section 16.1(d), shall constitute an immediate Event of Default without notice or opportunity to cure.

(d) **Insurance Defaults.** Five (5) Business Days after written notice from Lender to Borrower; provided that if the applicable policy has lapsed, Lender may obtain such insurance in accordance with Section 11.6 without further notice and the cost thereof shall constitute an advance under Section 9.14.

(e) **Substantial Completion Defaults.** No cure period; provided, however, that Lender may, in its reasonable discretion and upon Borrower's written request delivered before the Substantial Completion Deadline, extend the Substantial Completion Deadline by up to sixty (60) days in the aggregate on account of delays caused by events beyond Borrower's reasonable control (including casualty, governmental delay in the issuance of permits or certificates of occupancy, and labor disputes) that are not caused by any act, omission or breach of Borrower, Guarantor or the Contractor.

### 16.3 Lender's Right to Cure

Lender may, but shall have no obligation to, cure any default of Borrower under the Loan Documents. Any amounts expended by Lender in doing so shall constitute advances under Section 9.14, shall bear interest at the Default Rate and shall be secured by this Mortgage. Lender's exercise of this right shall not cure any Event of Default or waive any of Lender's rights.

### 16.4 Notice of Default as to Tenants

Borrower acknowledges that Lender may, following the occurrence and during the continuance of an Event of Default, deliver the notices to tenants contemplated by Section 3.3, and that such notices shall be effective upon delivery in accordance with the applicable Lease and Section 21.1.

## ARTICLE 17 — REMEDIES

### 17.1 Judicial Foreclosure; No Power of Sale

Upon the occurrence and during the continuance of an Event of Default, Lender may, in addition to all other rights and remedies available to it, foreclose this Mortgage in accordance with the laws of the State of South Carolina. Borrower acknowledges and agrees that the State of South Carolina is a judicial foreclosure jurisdiction and that this Mortgage does not, and shall not be construed to, grant Lender any power of sale, any right to sell the Property without judicial proceedings, or any other remedy not available to a mortgagee under the laws of the State of South Carolina. Any provision of this Mortgage that might be construed to grant a power of sale shall be deemed deleted and of no force or effect. Lender may also proceed to enforce the Note by an action at law for the indebtedness secured hereby, or may pursue any other remedy available to it, and may pursue such remedies concurrently or successively, in such order as Lender may elect, subject only to applicable law.

### 17.2 Receiver

Upon the occurrence and during the continuance of an Event of Default, Lender shall be entitled, without notice and without regard to the adequacy of any security for the Obligations, to the appointment of a receiver for the Property in any judicial proceeding to enforce this Mortgage, and Borrower consents to such appointment and agrees not to contest the same. Any receiver appointed shall have all powers and duties conferred by applicable law and by the order of appointment, including the power to manage the Property, collect the Rents, make repairs, and apply the net proceeds thereof as the court directs.

### 17.3 Remedies Under the UCC

Lender shall have all rights and remedies of a secured party under the UCC with respect to the Personal Property Collateral, including the rights set forth in Part 6 of Article 9 of the UCC, in addition to the rights and remedies provided in this Mortgage. Borrower agrees that ten (10) days' prior written notice of the time and place of any public sale or of the time after which any private sale or other disposition is to be made shall be commercially reasonable, and that any disposition of the Personal Property Collateral may be conducted on the Property. Lender may require Borrower to assemble the Personal Property Collateral and make it available to Lender at a place reasonably convenient to Lender.

### 17.4 Collection of Rents Following Default

Upon the occurrence and during the continuance of an Event of Default, Lender may exercise all rights under Article 3, including the right to collect the Rents directly, to notify tenants, and to enforce the Leases, in each case without the necessity of obtaining a court order, appointing a receiver or taking any other action, and the license granted to Borrower under Section 3.2 shall be automatically revoked.

### 17.5 Entry and Performance

Upon the occurrence and during the continuance of an Event of Default, Lender may enter upon and take possession of the Property, without notice, to perform any obligation of Borrower under the Loan Documents, to protect or preserve the Collateral, to make repairs and to complete the renovation, and may exclude Borrower, its agents and employees from the Property to the extent necessary to do so. Borrower authorizes Lender to take such actions and shall cooperate fully.

### 17.6 Application of Proceeds

The proceeds of any foreclosure sale, any collection of Rents, any sale of Personal Property Collateral and any other amounts received by Lender after an Event of Default shall be applied in the order of priority set forth in Section 5.5, and any surplus shall be paid to Borrower or to such other Person as may be entitled thereto by law.

### 17.7 Deficiency

If the proceeds of any foreclosure sale and the application of all other Collateral are insufficient to pay the Obligations in full, Lender may seek a deficiency judgment against Borrower and, to the extent provided in Article 18, against Guarantor, in accordance with applicable law. Nothing in this Section 17.7 shall limit or impair the obligations of Guarantor under the Guaranty, the Completion Guaranty, the Payment Guaranty or the Environmental Indemnity.

### 17.8 Cumulative Remedies; No Waiver

No right or remedy of Lender under the Loan Documents or applicable law is exclusive of any other right or remedy, and each shall be cumulative and in addition to every other right and remedy. No failure or delay by Lender in exercising any right, power or remedy shall operate as a waiver thereof, and no single or partial exercise shall preclude any other or further exercise. Any waiver by Lender shall be effective only if in writing and only to the extent expressly stated therein.

### 17.9 Waiver of Certain Rights; Non-Waivable Rights

To the maximum extent permitted by applicable law, Borrower waives (a) any right to a marshalling of assets or a sale in inverse order of alienation, (b) any appraisal, valuation, stay, extension, homestead, exemption or moratorium law now or hereafter in force, (c) any right to require Lender to proceed against any other Person or any other security before proceeding against the Property or Borrower, and (d) any notice of the occurrence of an Event of Default, of acceleration, of intent to foreclose, or of the time, place and terms of sale, except as expressly required by the Loan Documents or by applicable law that cannot be waived. Nothing in this Mortgage waives any right of Borrower or Guarantor that is non-waivable under applicable law, including any non-waivable statutory right or any right to notice required by applicable law.

### 17.10 Attorneys' Fees and Enforcement Costs

Borrower shall pay all costs and expenses, including reasonable attorneys' fees and disbursements, court costs, receiver's fees, appraisal fees, title search and title insurance charges, publication costs and trustee or commissioner fees, incurred by Lender in connection with the enforcement of the Loan Documents, the foreclosure of this Mortgage, the collection of the Obligations, any workout, forbearance, bankruptcy or insolvency proceeding, or the protection or preservation of the Collateral. All such amounts shall be secured by this Mortgage and shall bear interest at the Default Rate from the date of demand.

### 17.11 No Impairment of Security

Lender's acceptance of any payment after the due date, its failure to accelerate the Loan upon any Event of Default, its acceptance of a deed in lieu of foreclosure, its release of any portion of the Collateral, its modification of any Loan Document, its extension of the Maturity Date, or any other act or omission of Lender shall not release, impair or otherwise affect the lien of this Mortgage, the Assignment of Leases and Rents or the obligations of Borrower or Guarantor, except to the extent expressly provided in a written instrument executed by Lender.

    d = docx.Document(path)
    for i, t in enumerate(d.tables):

        tbl = t._tbl
        grid = tbl.find(qn('w:tblGrid'))
        for gc, width in zip(grid.findall(qn('w:gridCol')), w):
            gc.set(qn('w:w'), str(int(width*1440)))

# DRAFTING ISSUES MEMORANDUM

**PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT — PREPARED IN ANTICIPATION OF LITIGATION AND FOR THE PURPOSE OF RENDERING LEGAL ADVICE**

| | |
|---|---|
| **TO:** | Marcus Prideaux, Senior Vice President — Commercial Real Estate Lending, Calverley Heritage Bank |
| **FROM:** | Catherine A. Ashworth, Partner; Jordan Vickers, Associate — Fielding, Ashworth & Cole LLP |
| **DATE:** | April 1, 2025 |
| **RE:** | Issues memorandum accompanying first draft of Mortgage and Security Agreement — Calverley Heritage Bank / Palmetto Gateway Partners LLC, $14,750,000 loan (Deal Reference CHB CRE Loan No. 2025-CHS-0047); 520–534 King Street, Charleston, South Carolina 29403 |
| **ENCLOSURE:** | Mortgage and Security Agreement (first draft), 520–534 King Street, Charleston, SC |

## PART I — EXECUTIVE SUMMARY AND TOP-RISK REGISTER

The enclosed Mortgage and Security Agreement (the "**Draft Mortgage**") is a complete first draft prepared from the executed Term Sheet dated April 1, 2025 (the "**Term Sheet**"), the title commitment, the Phase I ESA executive summary, the redacted operating agreement summary, the rent roll and lease abstracts, the renovation budget and draw schedule, and the appraisal summary. It addresses every collateral, covenant, remedy and exhibit requirement appearing in those documents and resolves the principal drafting instructions in your March 18, 2025 markup notes.

The Draft Mortgage is, in our view, ready for internal review and borrower delivery **subject to the open items in Part VII**. Those items are not stylistic. Three of them bear directly on whether this loan should close in its current structure, and we ask that you address them with the loan committee before the draft is sent to borrower's counsel:

**1. The interest-only and DSCR structure cannot be satisfied at any achievable occupancy (Issue E-1).** On the numbers in the record, annual debt service after month 24 is approximately $1,124,239 (25-year amortization at 5.85%), and the best-case stabilized NOI in the borrower's own rent roll is $622,772 — a DSCR of approximately **0.55x** against a required 1.25x. Even interest-only, the ratio is 0.72x. To achieve 1.25x on amortizing debt service, NOI would need to be $1,405,299, or $45.33 per square foot on 31,000 square feet, versus market rents of $19.00–$28.00 per square foot. Even if all 31,000 square feet were leased at the rent roll's stabilized rents and the property carried **zero** operating expenses, gross revenue of $755,549 would produce a DSCR of only 0.67x. As currently structured, the DSCR covenant in Section 7.1 of the Term Sheet and Section 16.1(g) of the Draft Mortgage will be breached at the first test date and will generate an Event of Default on the second. Either the loan amount, the amortization, the interest-only period, the DSCR thresholds or the covenant itself must be re-cut, or the covenant must be supported by a debt service reserve, a cash sweep, an extended interest-shortfall guaranty and a cure mechanism. The Draft Mortgage includes a DSCR cure-deposit mechanism (Section 13.5) and a carve-out structure (Article 18), but those are mitigants, not a substitute for a commercially achievable covenant.

**2. SCDHEC issued a No Further Action letter dated August 12, 2021 (Site ID SC-29403-0772) subject to institutional controls recorded at Deed Book 1203, Page 89: (i) the ground floor of Lot 7 may not be used for residential purposes, and (ii) a vapor barrier beneath the Bay 1 slab must be maintained and periodically inspected, may not be penetrated without SCDHEC approval, and any work affecting the slab must include inspection and, where necessary, repair. The NFA status is contingent on continued compliance. The title company's closer note expressly directs that the Mortgage and the Environmental Indemnity "contain specific covenants addressing the SCDHEC land use restriction … including the vapor barrier maintenance and periodic inspection obligation and the prohibition on residential use," and that "the Mortgage should contain an event of default triggered by any failure to comply with … said land use restriction." The Phase I report makes the same recommendation (Section 6(d)).
*Draft treatment:* Article 12 is purpose-built rather than templated. §12.2(a)–(g) impose the use prohibition, the vapor barrier maintenance obligation (including annual and pre/post-construction inspection by a licensed environmental professional), advance SCDHEC notification, the requirement of Lender consent to any modification or vacation of the LUR, record-keeping and delivery obligations. §16.1(l) makes any failure an Event of Default; §18.2(d) makes it a springing full-recourse carve-out; §7.9 and §7.2(g) and §20.2(e) control work affecting the Bay 1 slab; Exhibit E sets out the LUR in full for the closing file.
*Recommendation:* Confirm the Environmental Indemnity (not in file) mirrors these obligations, as the title company requires both instruments to address the LUR. Note that the draft makes LUR non-compliance an Event of Default with **no cure period** because §16.2(c) is limited to SPE, transfer and bankruptcy defaults and §16.2(b) excludes nothing environmental — verify with you whether a short notice-and-cure period is preferable for an inadvertent administrative lapse (for example, a missed annual inspection report) as opposed to an actual slab penetration. Our view is that a 10-day notice period for reporting/inspection defaults, with no cure for use violations or unauthorized slab work, is the more defensible commercial position and is more likely to be accepted by borrower's counsel.

**B-2. The vapor barrier has never been inspected; the renovation scope may interface with the Bay 1 slab.**
*Record basis:* Phase I §5.3 (vapor barrier "not directly visible or inspectable"; recommends confirmation by a licensed environmental professional "prior to or promptly after acquisition, and particularly before any renovation activity affecting the Bay 1 floor slab"); Phase I §5.4 note regarding planned renovation; Renovation Budget lines 1.0 (HVAC) and 3.0 (façade).
*Analysis:* The Phase I recommends a pre- or post-acquisition inspection. The renovation involves rooftop HVAC replacement and ductwork, elevator modernization, and façade work. Ductwork distribution and any slab-adjacent work could require penetration of or access through the Bay 1 slab. If the vapor barrier is compromised, the NFA determination is at risk and SCDHEC may reopen the file, with remediation cost potentially at the owner's expense.
*Draft treatment:* §12.2(c) requires a pre-construction inspection, a post-construction inspection and annual inspections thereafter; §7.9 prohibits slab-affecting work without SCDHEC notice, Lender consent and a consultant's plan.
*Recommendation:* Add a closing condition (or a 30-day post-closing covenant with a holdback of a portion of the Holdback) requiring a baseline vapor barrier inspection report. We recommend the former; if the borrower resists a pre-closing condition, the latter is a reasonable fallback. Also confirm with the Contractor, in writing, that the HVAC and elevator scopes do not require Bay 1 slab penetration; if they do, the notification and consent protocol must be sequenced into the draw schedule.

**B-3. The environmental record is an executive summary, not a report, and the Phase II waiver is documented only by reference.**
*Record basis:* Phase I cover notice, §§1 (limitations), 8 (qualifications); Term Sheet §12.1(c); Phase I §6 note (waiver documented in correspondence dated January 22, 2025 between Mr. Prideaux and Clearfield).
*Analysis:* The Phase I document in the file states that it "is extracted from the full Phase I," that the full report "should be reviewed in its entirety," and that the summary "does not constitute a complete Phase I Environmental Site Assessment under ASTM E1527-21 or 40 CFR Part 312." Lender's record should contain the full report, including Appendix A (database search), Appendix B (aerial photographs), Appendix C (Sanborn maps) and Appendix E (interviews), both for credit file purposes and to support the bona fide prospective purchaser / innocent landowner posture that depends on all appropriate inquiries.
*Draft treatment:* §8.5 limits Borrower's environmental representations to matters disclosed in the Phase I Report and Exhibit E (so Borrower does not warrant more than the record supports), and §12.3 states expressly that Lender's waiver of a Phase II assessment is not a representation as to environmental condition.
*Recommendation:* Obtain the full report and a reliance letter naming Lender and Borrower as intended users; place the January 22, 2025 waiver correspondence in the credit file.
MD

tool_calls.name: bash
tool_calls.arguments:
{"command": "cd /workspace && cat >> work/memo.md << 'MD'

### C. Leases, rents and tenant matters

**C-1. The assignment of rents is drafted as an absolute and present assignment, and the "collateral assignment" vocabulary has been removed throughout.**
*Record basis:* Term Sheet §5.2 (absolute assignment; may be included in the Mortgage or executed separately); Prior Counsel Notes §3 (directing absolute assignment under the Uniform Assignment of Rents Act; removal of "collateral" characterization); Title Commitment Requirement 5 (assignment of leases and rents or inclusion within the Mortgage).
*Analysis:* The Mortgage incorporates the assignment rather than requiring a separate recorded instrument, which reduces recording cost and centralizes enforcement — the approach your markup notes directed. Perfection follows from recording (§3.1); enforcement follows default and notice (§3.3). The license to collect before default (§3.2) preserves Borrower's ordinary-course operation while making clear that collection after default requires no receiver, no court order and no tenant consent.
*Draft treatment:* Article 3. §3.1 characterizes the transfer as absolute and present, cites the South Carolina Uniform Assignment of Rents Act (S.C. Code Ann. § 29-3-100 *et seq.*, as cited in your markup notes) and states that perfection occurs upon recording. §§3.2–3.4 provide the revocable license, notice and enforcement mechanics, and security deposit treatment. §3.7 prevents merger of the assignment into the lien on foreclosure.
*Recommendation:* Have the statutory citation verified against the current Code before execution. We have retained the citation exactly as it appeared in your markup notes; we have not independently confirmed the section numbering of the South Carolina enactment, and an incorrect pin cite in a recorded instrument is an avoidable distraction. Also confirm whether the Trust Fund provisions of the Lease trigger any separate treatment of security deposits.

**C-2. The Lowcountry Provisions lease has no assignment provision, no estoppel obligation and no SNDA — yet estoppels and SNDAs from all tenants are conditions precedent.**
*Record basis:* Rent Roll, Lease Abstracts tab ("Assignment/Subletting: No provision… does not contain a consent requirement, prohibition, or landlord approval mechanism"; "Lease does not contain a provision requiring tenant to deliver estoppel certificates"; "Lease does not contain SNDA provisions"); Term Sheet §§2.3 (estoppels and SNDAs required), 12.1(j), 12.1(k); Title Commitment Requirement 11 and Closer Note 5; Prior Counsel Notes §3 (identifying this as critical).
*Analysis:* This tenant occupies 3,800 square feet at $28.50 per square foot (escalating to $30.24 by January 2027) through December 31, 2027, with a five-year renewal option exercisable by March 31, 2027 — a notice date that falls before the first DSCR test and within the lockout period. It has no contractual obligation to deliver an estoppel or an SNDA, and no contractual machinery for assignment consent. Legally, the rent assignment is enforceable on notice under the Act; practically, a cooperative tenant at closing is worth more than a correct legal position, and the last thing the bank needs in a workout is a tenant asserting that it never agreed to pay a lender. The lease also carries an exclusive use (specialty grocery) that constrains future leasing, and the tenant's renewal notice deadline should be diarized.
*Draft treatment:* §3.5 requires estoppels and SNDAs from each of the three tenants as a condition to the initial advance and specifies that the Lowcountry estoppel must acknowledge the Mortgage and the assignment, confirm no offsets, and agree to pay Rents to Lender on notice; §9.7 imposes a post-closing estoppel covenant; §20.1(l) makes delivery a condition precedent; §3.5 also includes the post-closing covenant (per your instruction) to pursue a consent-to-assignment amendment at the next renewal, extension or amendment opportunity. §20.3 requires any waiver of a condition to be in writing and to identify the condition waived.
*Recommendation:* Begin the estoppel and SNDA process now, using Lender's form with the Mortgage and assignment attached. If the tenant will not sign an SNDA, our recommended fallback is (i) an estoppel containing an acknowledgment of the assignment and a direction to pay, plus (ii) a Lender notice letter to the tenant under the Act, plus (iii) a written, specific Lender waiver of the SNDA condition under §20.3. Do not permit the condition to be waived informally by closing.

**C-3. The Harmon & Wren right of first refusal on Bay 2 governs the lease-up schedule on which the whole credit story depends.**
*Record basis:* Rent Roll, Lease Abstracts and Vacancy Schedule tabs (ROFR: 15 business days to accept or decline; survives renewal; est. 60–90 days added to Bay 2 absorption); Appraisal §3.2 and §6.3 (same conclusion); Term Sheet §10.6.
*Analysis:* Bay 2 (3,800 square feet) is one of only two vacant spaces and is the space the borrower projects to lease first (execution projected October 2025, rent commencement January 1, 2026). The ROFR gives Harmon & Wren a 15-business-day right to match any third-party offer, and the tenant's own lease expires June 30, 2026 with a renewal notice deadline of December 31, 2025 — meaning the borrower will be negotiating the renewal and running a Bay 2 marketing process at the same time, with the ROFR as leverage. The tenant's early termination right (effective June 30, 2025, notice deadline December 31, 2024) appears to have lapsed; that should be confirmed in the estoppel.
*Draft treatment:* §9.6 requires compliance with the ROFR and the Lowcountry exclusivity, requires Lender consent to any new lease or modification over 5,000 square feet or over five years, and requires delivery of credit information before execution. §8.4 requires the rent roll representation to capture ROFRs and exclusives. §13.3(c) requires certified quarterly rent rolls with a delinquency schedule.
*Recommendation:* Ask Borrower to confirm in writing that the Harmon & Wren termination right has lapsed, and to provide a leasing plan for Bay 2 that assumes the ROFR process runs in parallel. Consider whether the Lender's consent right over new leases should extend to all ground-floor retail bays rather than only those over 5,000 square feet — at 3,800 square feet per bay, the current threshold means no ground-floor lease requires Lender consent.

**C-4. Tenant improvement funding has two possible sources, and the draft fixes the order of priority.**
*Record basis:* Term Sheet §§6.3 (separate $150,000 reserve, replenished within 30 days of demand, exclusive use for tenant improvements and leasing commissions), 8.2 (Renovation Budget line 4.0, $550,000 of TI allowances); Renovation Budget lines 4.0 and 5.0; Vacancy Schedule (TI cost $310,600 and leasing commissions $89,750 in the worst case).
*Analysis:* Without an ordering rule, the same tenant improvement dollar could be claimed twice — from the TI/LC reserve and from the Holdback — and the reserve's 30-day replenishment obligation could collide with Borrower's $500,000 liquidity covenant. The projected leasing commissions ($89,750 worst case) are not in the Renovation Budget at all and must come from the reserve.
*Draft treatment:* §6.3(d) requires tenant improvement costs to be funded first from the TI/LC reserve and then from the Holdback, and prohibits double reimbursement; §6.3(c) imposes the 30-day replenishment obligation and §16.1(h) makes failure an Event of Default; §7.2(f) conditions TI-related draws on an approved lease.
*Recommendation:* Confirm the allocation with Borrower and reflect it in the closing statement. Note the interaction between replenishment and the liquidity covenant in §13.2 and consider whether the replenishment obligation should be subordinate to maintenance of the liquidity covenant.

**C-5. Leasing consent thresholds are drawn from the Term Sheet and should be reviewed against the actual space configuration.**
*Record basis:* Term Sheet §10.6 (consent for leases over 5,000 square feet or over five years, not unreasonably withheld, conditioned or delayed).
*Analysis:* All three retail bays are 3,800 square feet and the two office suites are 9,800 square feet. The 5,000 square foot threshold therefore means no ground-floor retail lease requires Lender consent, while any office lease does. Renewals may constitute new leases for this purpose, and all three leases have renewal options.
*Draft treatment:* §9.6 tracks the Term Sheet thresholds and adds the compliance carve-outs for the LUR, tenant exclusives and purchase options, and gives Lender a 10-business-day pre-execution review of leases requiring consent.
*Recommendation:* Decide whether the thresholds are intended as drafted (we have not changed them, because they are commercial terms in an executed commitment).

**C-6. The in-place rent figure in the Term Sheet, the appraisal and the rent roll is stale, and the occupancy figure is wrong.**
*Record basis:* Term Sheet §2.3 (68% occupancy; "$415,100" total in-place rent; vacant space "13,600 square feet, or approximately 43.9%"); Appraisal §1 and §3.1 (68%; 21,400 square feet; $19.40 per square foot weighted average); Rent Roll, Summary tab (56.13% occupancy; $415,100; $23.86 per square foot) and Lease Abstracts tab (escalation schedules showing Lowcountry at $29.36 per square foot from January 2025 and Harmon & Wren at $25.22 per square foot from July 2024).
*Analysis:* Three separate problems. First, occupancy: occupied area is 17,400 square feet (3,800 + 3,800 + 9,800) — 56.13% of 31,000 square feet. The Term Sheet's 68% is internally inconsistent with its own statement that 13,600 square feet (43.9%) is vacant. The appraisal's "21,400 SF" does not correspond to any combination of leased spaces in the rent roll and appears to be the source of both the 68% figure and the $19.40 per square foot weighted average (since $415,100 ÷ 21,400 = $19.40). Second, rent: the $415,100 figure reflects pre-escalation rents. Applying the contractual escalations, in-place rent at closing is approximately $422,966 (Lowcountry $111,549 at $29.36 per square foot; Harmon & Wren $95,817 at $25.22 per square foot; Tidemark $215,600 at $22.00 per square foot, with its first escalation not until April 1, 2026). The rent roll is internally inconsistent on this point: the Summary tab shows $28.50 and $24.00 as "Current" while the Lease Abstracts tab shows the escalated schedule. Third, the same underlying error appears in the appraiser's weighted average rent, which understates in-place rent per square foot by $4.46.
*Draft treatment:* The Draft Mortgage does not embed any occupancy percentage or aggregate rent figure. §8.4 requires a representation measured against a **certified** rent roll attached as Exhibit D (Schedule D-1), §13.4 requires occupancy reporting with each compliance certificate, and §13.3(c) requires certified quarterly rent rolls with delinquency detail. Exhibit D's summary table reflects the base rents as stated in the rent roll, with commencement and escalation detail moved into the accompanying notes so that the exhibit does not assert a figure the record cannot support.
*Recommendation:* Obtain a certified rent roll as of the closing date, reconciled to the leases including escalations, and use it as Schedule D-1. The corrected occupancy and rent figures should also be reflected in the credit file and in any loan committee presentation, because the 68% figure materially overstates the Property's leased position.

**C-7. Security deposits and tenant funds are assigned but must remain available to tenants.**
*Record basis:* Rent Roll ($69,183 held); Term Sheet §5.1(d) and §5.2; Prior Counsel Notes §3.
*Draft treatment:* §3.1 assigns security deposits; §3.4 requires Borrower to hold them in accordance with the Leases and applicable law, not to apply them except as the Lease permits, and to deliver a schedule and, on default, transfer them to Lender's control.
*Recommendation:* No action, other than to confirm that the certified rent roll's deposit figures reconcile to Borrower's rent ledger at closing.

### D. Single-purpose entity, organizational authority and bankruptcy remoteness

**D-1. The Operating Agreement does not satisfy the Term Sheet's SPE requirements, and the amendment must be signed by all three Members.**
*Record basis:* Term Sheet §§10.1(a)–(g), 11.1(j), 12.1(g); OA Summary §§1.4, 3.1, 3.2, 8.1, 9.1; Prior Counsel Notes §4.
*Analysis:* The Operating Agreement summary confirms each deficiency your markup notes identified: no independent manager or independent director (OA Summary §3.1); no separateness covenants and no requirement that the Company maintain itself as an entity separate from its Members; a purpose clause with an unlimited "any and all activities necessary, incidental, or related thereto" catch-all (§1.4); no lender consent to dissolution and no bankruptcy-consent provision (§8.1); and amendments requiring the Managing Member plus 75% of membership interests (§9.1). Because GDG holds 72%, GDG cannot amend the Operating Agreement alone: **at least one Passive Member must approve the amendment**, and the amendment must be executed by all three Members. Your markup notes correctly identified this and required execution by all three.
*Draft treatment:* Article 14 sets out the single-purpose purpose limitation, the eleven separateness covenants, the Independent Manager requirement (including consent to bankruptcy, dissolution, merger and amendment of SPE provisions), the Member consent obligation and the prohibition on amending organizational documents; §14.6 records the specific deficiencies in the Operating Agreement as delivered so that the amendment can be tested against them; §8.6 requires a representation that the Operating Agreement complies from and after closing; §20.1(i) makes the executed amendment a condition precedent; Article 23 contains Member signature blocks.
*Recommendation:* Circulate a form of Operating Agreement Amendment (we have not drafted it — it is not within the scope of the enclosed deliverable) and require executed originals from Graydon Development Group LLC, Tidewater Opportunity Fund II LP and Harborline Capital Advisors LLC. Note that Section 9.1 of the Operating Agreement permits amendment with 75% approval **except** where the amendment alters a Member's economic rights or increases capital obligations, in which case each affected Member must consent. The SPE provisions should not alter economics, but confirm that with borrower's counsel so the amendment does not require unanimous consent on a different basis.

**D-2. Execution of a $14,750,000 loan is itself a Major Decision requiring 75% Member approval.**
*Record basis:* OA Summary §3.2(ii) ("Any financing or refinancing of the Property in an amount in excess of $1,000,000" is a Major Decision requiring 75% of membership interests), §3.1(e) (Managing Member may execute loan documents), §3.3 (no officers appointed; documents executed by Mr. Graydon as sole member and manager of GDG); Term Sheet §12.1(h) (opinion as to due authorization); Title Commitment Requirement 8(b) and (c).
*Analysis:* There is a tension in the organizational documents. Section 3.1(e) gives the Managing Member power to execute loan documents, but Section 3.2(ii) makes financing in excess of $1,000,000 a Major Decision requiring 75% approval, which GDG's 72% cannot deliver alone. A lender relying only on the Managing Member's signature may be relying on authority that is internally conditioned. Title Requirement 8(b) requires satisfactory evidence that the executing persons are authorized "pursuant to the operating agreement and/or resolutions of the members," and the Term Sheet requires an opinion that execution is duly authorized.
*Draft treatment:* §8.2 contains a representation of due authorization "including by Graydon Development Group LLC as Managing Member and by the Members to the extent required by the Operating Agreement"; the Members' Consent in Article 23 constitutes the written consent of all three Members to the execution and delivery of **this Mortgage**.
*Recommendation:* The Article 23 consent is limited to the Mortgage. We recommend replacing it at closing with a single omnibus written consent of all Members authorizing the Loan and all Loan Documents (Note, Mortgage, Assignment, UCC filings, Environmental Indemnity, and acknowledgment of the Guaranties), and that Borrower's counsel's opinion expressly address compliance with Section 3.2(ii) of the Operating Agreement. This is a five-minute fix at closing and a difficult problem to cure later.

**D-3. Tidewater GP Holdings LLC must be shown to have authority to bind the fund.**
*Record basis:* OA Summary §§2.1 ("Tidewater GP Holdings LLC has the exclusive authority to manage and direct the affairs of Tidewater"), 10 (signature blocks); Prior Counsel Notes §4 (asking for a GP authorization certificate).
*Analysis:* The limited partnership agreement of Tidewater Opportunity Fund II LP is not in the file, so we cannot confirm whether its general partner may bind the fund to an SPE amendment and member consent without further fund-level approvals.
*Draft treatment:* Article 23 signature block for Tidewater is executed by Tidewater GP Holdings LLC as general partner.
*Recommendation:* Obtain a general partner authorization certificate or resolution, or the relevant provisions of the limited partnership agreement, before closing.

**D-4. The registered agent is identified differently in two source documents.**
*Record basis:* Term Sheet §1.2 ("Capitol Registered Agents Inc., 1201 Main Street, Suite 410, Columbia"); OA Summary §1.3 ("Statehouse Registered Agents, Inc., 1201 Main Street, Suite 410, Columbia").
*Analysis:* Same address, different entity name. One of the two is wrong, or the agent was changed. The Draft Mortgage does not name the registered agent; it requires notice of any change (§9.13(g)) and prohibits change without notice (§10.6).
*Recommendation:* Confirm current registered agent from the South Carolina Secretary of State business entity filing before closing, and correct whichever source document is wrong for the credit file.

### E. Loan economics

**E-1. The DSCR covenant cannot be satisfied at any occupancy, on the borrower's own projections.**
*Record basis:* Term Sheet §§7.1 (1.25x minimum, testing from month 24), 11.1(i) (two consecutive quarters below 1.25x is an Event of Default); Rent Roll, Vacancy Schedule tab (stabilized best-case NOI $622,772; debt service $93,500 per month / $1,122,000 per year; DSCR 0.555x; "DOES NOT MEET 1.25x COVENANT"; realistic scenario NOI $314,782; DSCR 0.281x).
*Analysis:* We recomputed the debt service rather than adopting the workbook's figure: 25-year amortization of $14,750,000 at 5.85% produces $93,686.61 per month and $1,124,239 per year. Against best-case stabilized NOI of $622,772, that is a DSCR of **0.554x**; on an interest-only basis, $622,772 ÷ $862,875 = **0.722x**; on the workbook's "realistic" scenario, **0.280x**. The requirement of 1.25x on amortizing debt service implies required NOI of **$1,405,299**, or $45.33 per square foot across 31,000 square feet, against market rents of $24.00–$32.00 per square foot for ground-floor retail and $19.00–$25.00 per square foot for Class B office. Even with all 31,000 square feet leased at the rent roll's stabilized rents ($755,549 of gross revenue) and zero operating expenses, the DSCR would be 0.672x. There is no occupancy outcome that satisfies the covenant. This is not a lease-up timing risk; it is a structural mismatch between the loan amount, the debt service and the Property's income.
*Draft treatment:* §13.1 defines DSCR, Net Operating Income and Annual Debt Service with the specificity the Term Sheet leaves open (Term Sheet §7.1: "The precise definitions … shall be set forth in the Loan Documents"); Net Operating Income excludes non-recurring items, insurance and condemnation proceeds, capital expenditures and expenses funded from reserves, caps management fees at 4% of gross revenue, and Annual Debt Service is calculated on the 25-year amortization at the greater of the current rate and the floor rate. §13.1(d) grosses up debt service to the full $14,750,000 even before full disbursement. §13.5 provides a cure-deposit mechanism (a deposit equal to the NOI shortfall divided by 0.125, released after two consecutive compliant test dates). §16.1(g) implements the Term Sheet's two-quarter default trigger.
*Recommendation:* This requires a credit decision, not a drafting decision. The options, in order of structural soundness: (i) reduce the loan amount or extend the interest-only period so that the covenant is achievable on stabilized NOI; (ii) replace the amortizing DSCR test with an interest-only DSCR test at a lower threshold (for example, 1.00x on interest-only debt service, which still implies required NOI of $862,875 — itself 39% above the best-case projection); (iii) retain the covenant but require a funded debt service reserve equal to 12 months of debt service plus an extended interest-shortfall guaranty running beyond the first test date; (iv) require a cash sweep at any DSCR below 1.10x with a hard lockbox. As drafted, the Loan will be in default by the second test date absent one of these changes, and a covenant that the lender knows will be breached is worse than no covenant — it invites a waiver practice and, in a bankruptcy, an argument that the lender never expected compliance.

**E-2. The appraisal's income approach cannot be reconciled to its value conclusions, and the loan is sized at 81.04% of the as-is value.**
*Record basis:* Appraisal §§6.2 (as-is NOI approximately $332,000–$345,000; 6.25% cap rate; value $18,200,000), 6.3 (stabilized NOI $582,000–$592,000; 5.85% cap rate; value $23,500,000), 7 (final value opinions), 8 (limiting conditions); Term Sheet §§2.4, 3.5, 12.1(d); RTC/FIRREA references in Term Sheet §2.4.
*Analysis:* Applying the appraiser's own selected cap rates to the appraiser's own NOI produces values of approximately $5.42 million (as-is, $338,500 ÷ 6.25%) and $10.03 million (as-stabilized, $587,000 ÷ 5.85%). Conversely, the stated values imply cap rates of approximately 1.86% and 2.50%. Those are not plausible going-in cap rates for Upper King Street mixed-use property in a market where the appraisal itself reports market cap rates of 5.75%–6.50%. The sales comparison approach, by contrast, is internally consistent: $18,200,000 ÷ 31,000 square feet = $587 per square foot against comparables at $550, $600 and $620 per square foot. The most likely explanation is that the income approach was not reconciled to the rent roll, or that the reported NOI figures are wrong — which is consistent with the same document's occupancy and weighted-average-rent errors identified in Issue C-6. Either way, the loan is sized at 81.04% of a value whose income-approach support we cannot verify, on a property whose projected NOI would support roughly $10 million of value at the appraiser's own stabilized cap rate.
*Draft treatment:* The Draft Mortgage does not recite values; §20.1(g) conditions the initial advance on receipt of an appraisal supporting the as-is and as-stabilized values and on evidence of any approved exception to underwriting guidelines; §9.12 preserves Lender's right to obtain appraisals at Borrower's expense.
*Recommendation:* Order a USPAP Standard 3 review of the appraisal before closing and require the appraiser to reconcile the income approach to the rent roll or explain the variance. We make no representation as to value and have not performed an appraisal; our point is internal consistency, which is squarely within the lender's diligence obligations under its appraisal regulations. This finding should be presented to loan committee together with Issue E-1.

**E-3. Sources and uses do not balance after transaction costs.**
*Record basis:* Term Sheet §§3.3 (initial advance applied to purchase price, closing costs and reserves), 3.4 (Total Project Cost $20,950,000; equity $6,200,000), 13.1 (origination fee $147,500), 13.2 (Borrower pays all Lender costs), 6.3 ($150,000 reserve at closing); Prior Counsel Notes §6 (0.37% mortgage tax; $54,575).
*Analysis:* Total sources are $20,950,000 (Loan $14,750,000 + equity $6,200,000). Total uses per the Term Sheet are also $20,950,000 — purchase price plus Renovation Budget — which by definition excludes the origination fee, the recording fee, title premium, survey, appraisal, environmental, UCC filings, Lender's legal fees and the $150,000 TI/LC reserve. Because $900,000 of equity is committed to renovation (Renovation Budget, Budget Detail tab), only $5,300,000 of equity is available at closing; $12,500,000 + $5,300,000 = $17,800,000, exactly the purchase price, leaving nothing for costs. The identifiable shortfall before unquantified items is $352,075 ($147,500 + $54,575 + $150,000).
*Draft treatment:* §20.1(n) conditions the initial advance on receipt of the $6,200,000 equity contribution "together with a sources and uses statement for the Loan acceptable to Lender"; §22.9 allocates recording fees, documentary taxes and closing costs to Borrower.
*Recommendation:* Require Borrower to fund additional equity of not less than the shortfall, or obtain written confirmation from Prestige Title of the complete closing statement and Borrower's evidence of funds. This is a closing-mechanics item that becomes a funding failure on the closing date if it is not addressed now.

**E-4. The yield maintenance formula in the Term Sheet is under-specified, and the formula in your markup notes differs from it.**
*Record basis:* Term Sheet §4.2 (premium equals the greater of 1.00% of the outstanding principal or the present value of the excess of interest at the Note rate over interest at "the treasury rate plus fifty (50) basis points," discounted "at the treasury rate"); Prior Counsel Notes §5 (proposing a formula equal to the present value of remaining payments discounted at the Treasury Rate less the principal prepaid, with "in no event … less than zero," and recommending that the 50 basis points be added to the loan rate rather than the Treasury rate).
*Analysis:* Two drafting positions were available. The Term Sheet's structure is a "greater of" test with a hard 1.00% floor; the markup note's structure is a present-value differential with a zero floor and no minimum. Those produce different premiums, and the markup note's version drops the 1.00% floor that appears in the executed commitment. The markup note also flags the ambiguity in "treasury rate + 50 bps" and recommends adding the spread to the loan rate; the Term Sheet's text, read naturally, adds it to the Treasury rate in computing the comparison yield.
*Draft treatment:* We followed the Term Sheet. §5.8 states the "greater of" test with the 1.00% minimum preserved; §5.9 sets out a step-by-step computation, defines the Treasury Rate by reference to Federal Reserve Statistical Release H.15 — Treasury Constant Maturities with linear interpolation between the two nearest published maturities, measured as of the second Business Day preceding prepayment, on an actual/360 basis with monthly compounding, treats the interest differential as floored at zero (so the computation under limb (ii) cannot be negative), and requires Lender to deliver its computation within five Business Days.
*Recommendation:* Obtain a written instruction from you on two points before the draft goes to borrower: (i) whether the 50 basis points is added to the Treasury rate (as drafted, consistent with the Term Sheet's text) or to the Note rate (as your markup notes recommended); and (ii) whether the 1.00% minimum is retained (as drafted and as the Term Sheet requires) or dropped (as the markup note formula implies). We recommend retaining both as drafted. South Carolina courts have enforced yield maintenance provisions that are mathematically determinate; the risk of unenforceability arises from ambiguity, and the drafted formula is designed to eliminate it.

**E-5. Prepayment during the lockout is addressed inconsistently in the Term Sheet.**
*Record basis:* Term Sheet §§4.1 ("The Loan may not be prepaid… during the first twenty-four (24) months"; any prepayment "in violation of this restriction shall be subject to a prepayment premium as described in Section 4.2"), 4.2 (premium applies "from the expiration of the Lockout Period through the forty-eighth (48th) month").
*Analysis:* Section 4.1 prohibits prepayment during the lockout but then says a prohibited prepayment is subject to a Section 4.2 premium — and Section 4.2 by its terms applies only after the lockout expires. A pure prohibition (with no premium, because no prepayment may occur) and a prohibition-with-premium produce different negotiating positions and different outcomes if a borrower tenders funds.
*Draft treatment:* §5.7 prohibits voluntary prepayment during the lockout, permits Lender to refuse and return any tendered amount, and provides that if Lender accepts in its sole discretion, the premium equals the amount that would be payable under §5.8 had the prepayment occurred on the last day of the lockout.
*Recommendation:* Confirm this treatment, and confirm the casualty and condemnation carve-out in §5.7 and §15.3(c) (proceeds applied at par without premium). Your markup notes asked us to confirm that carve-out with the client; the Term Sheet is silent, and we have taken the borrower-favorable position because an involuntary prepayment premium is difficult to defend as liquidated damages.

**E-6. Interest mechanics are not specified in the Term Sheet.**
*Record basis:* Term Sheet §3.6 (Daily SOFR plus 2.85%; floor of 3.00%; published rate or prior Business Day's rate).
*Analysis:* The Term Sheet does not specify the day-count convention (actual/360 versus actual/365), whether interest is compounded, how partial accrual periods are handled, or what happens if Daily SOFR is permanently discontinued. Each has a real cost effect: actual/360 produces approximately 1.4% more interest than actual/365 on the same nominal rate.
*Draft treatment:* §5.2(b) adopts actual/360 daily accrual; §5.2(c) makes Lender's determination conclusive absent manifest error and requires a monthly rate statement; §5.2(d) provides a successor-rate mechanism (New York Fed recommended successor rate plus any recommended spread adjustment, giving effect to the floor).
*Recommendation:* Confirm actual/360 with you and with the loan servicing group; document the convention in the Note and the loan system so that billing matches documentation.

**E-7. The default rate and late charge should be reviewed for enforceability.**
*Record basis:* Term Sheet §§3.7 (default rate = applicable rate + 5.00%), 3.11 (5% late charge after 10 calendar days).
*Analysis:* At the SOFR floor, the default rate is 10.85%. South Carolina permits parties to agree upon rates for commercial loan transactions above certain thresholds, but the combination of a 5.00% default spread, a 5% late charge and compounding default interest can attract a penalty characterization in a contested enforcement, particularly if the late charge is imposed on the same amounts that are also carrying default interest.
*Draft treatment:* §§5.3 (default rate), 5.4 (late charge, with express statement that it compensates administrative expense and is not a penalty), 5.13 (usury savings clause that limits the aggregate to the maximum lawful rate, applies any excess to principal, and provides for pro rata allocation over the term).
*Recommendation:* Confirm with South Carolina counsel that the 10.85% default rate and the 5% late charge are enforceable as drafted; we have included the savings clause as a backstop but have not rendered an opinion on the maximum lawful rate.

**E-8. The interest-shortfall guaranty ends twelve months before the first DSCR test.**
*Record basis:* Term Sheet §§5.5(c) (shortfall guaranty covering "the first fourteen (14) months following closing"), 7.1 (DSCR testing from month 24), 8.3 (Substantial Completion June 15, 2026).
*Analysis:* Fourteen months from April 15, 2025 is June 15, 2026. The first DSCR test date under the Term Sheet is the quarter ending June 30, 2027. Between June 15, 2026 and June 30, 2027 there is no debt service support collateral, no DSCR covenant in effect, and no occupancy requirement — during exactly the period in which Suite B is projected to be leased (projected rent commencement February 1, 2027, only 2.5 months before the test date, which the workbook itself describes as an "AGGRESSIVE TIMELINE").
*Draft treatment:* §19.1 recites the Payment Guaranty on the Term Sheet's 14-month terms (we have not extended a commercial term); Article 18 contains the carve-out recourse structure; §13.1 commences DSCR testing with the quarter ending June 30, 2027, consistent with the Term Sheet.
*Recommendation:* Extend the interest-shortfall guaranty to the first DSCR test date (or to achievement of 90% occupancy), or add a funded interest reserve for the intervening period. This is the cheapest available mitigation for Issues E-1 and E-2 and should be negotiated as a package.

**E-9. The Term Sheet describes the Guaranty as "full recourse" and simultaneously as a non-recourse carve-out guaranty.**
*Record basis:* Term Sheet §5.5 (introducing "a full recourse personal guaranty," then describing "(a) Non-Recourse Carve-Out Guaranty" — the Loan to be "structured as non-recourse to Borrower, except for certain 'carve-out' events … that trigger springing full recourse liability of Guarantor for the entire outstanding indebtedness" — plus (b) the Completion Guaranty and (c) the Payment Guaranty); Guarantor Acknowledgment (referring to "the Guaranty Agreement, Completion Guaranty, Payment Guaranty"); Term Sheet §§14.3 (Loan Document list includes only a "Guaranty Agreement").
*Analysis:* The document uses "full recourse" in two different senses: full recourse as to the amount of liability once a carve-out is triggered (springing full recourse), and full recourse as to the circumstances of liability (a payment guaranty of all obligations at all times). Which is intended determines whether Guarantor is liable for ordinary payment defaults or only for bad-boy acts plus the completion and shortfall guaranties. The document list compounds the ambiguity by naming one "Guaranty Agreement" in §14.3 while the acknowledgment names three instruments.
*Draft treatment:* Article 18 implements the carve-out structure (non-recourse to Borrower subject to springing full recourse to Borrower and Guarantor for the entire Obligations upon a Carve-Out Event, mirroring Term Sheet §5.5(a)(i)–(v) with sub-clauses); §19.1 recites the three separate guaranties; §19.7 resolves conflicts among Loan Documents.
*Recommendation:* Confirm the guaranty structure and the number of guaranty instruments, and conform the document list in Term Sheet §14.3 and the closing checklist. If the Guaranty is intended to be a payment guaranty of all Obligations at all times, Article 18 should be revised and the recourse analysis changes materially.

### F. Renovation and draw administration

**F-1. The draw schedule does not reconcile to the budget.**
*Record basis:* Renovation Budget and Draw Schedule, Budget Detail and Draw Schedule tabs.
*Analysis:* Summing the 14 monthly draws by line item and comparing to the Budget Detail allocation:

| Line item | Budget | Lender Holdback per budget | Borrower equity per budget | Draws: Lender | Draws: Borrower | Draws total | Variance vs budget |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| HVAC | $1,200,000 | $850,000 | $350,000 | $900,000 | $350,000 | $1,250,000 | **+$50,000** |
| Elevator | $475,000 | $375,000 | $100,000 | $325,000 | $100,000 | $425,000 | **–$50,000** |
| Façade | $625,000 | $425,000 | $200,000 | $425,000 | $200,000 | $625,000 | $0 |
| TI allowances | $550,000 | $450,000 | $100,000 | $450,000 | $110,000 | $560,000 | **+$10,000** |
| Soft costs/contingency | $300,000 | $150,000 | $150,000 | $150,000 | $145,000 | $295,000 | **–$5,000** |
| **Total** | **$3,150,000** | **$2,250,000** | **$900,000** | **$2,250,000** | **$905,000** | **$3,155,000** | **+$5,000** |

The Holdback total ($2,250,000) is correct, but Borrower equity is overstated by $5,000 ($905,000 drawn against a $900,000 commitment), and the schedule's final row shows remaining equity of –$5,000. HVAC holdback draws also exceed the line-item allocation by $50,000, offset by a $50,000 shortfall in elevator draws.
*Draft treatment:* Exhibit C adopts the Budget Detail allocation and states that the draw schedule is a planning document that does not amend the budget or waive any condition; §7.2(e) requires evidence that Borrower is funding its proportionate share consistent with Exhibit C; §7.5 requires Borrower to fund cost overruns.
*Recommendation:* Have Borrower reconcile and re-certify the draw schedule before closing. Do not attach the current version as Schedule C-1 without correction.

**F-2. The draw schedule ignores the 10% retainage, so the Borrower must fund about $225,000 more during construction than the schedule shows.**
*Record basis:* Term Sheet §8.4 (10% retainage until substantial completion); Renovation Budget and Draw Schedule (holdback fully drawn by Month 14).
*Analysis:* Ten percent of the $2,250,000 Holdback is $225,000. If retainage is withheld, aggregate disbursements before Substantial Completion cannot exceed $2,025,000. The schedule reaches cumulative holdback draws of $2,235,000 by Month 13 (May 15, 2026) and $2,250,000 by Month 14, which exceeds the 90% ceiling by up to $225,000. Because substantial completion is a condition to release, the schedule's assumption that the Holdback is exhausted at the substantial completion date is arithmetically inconsistent with the retainage requirement.
*Draft treatment:* §7.3 states the retainage requirement and expressly states the $2,025,000 ceiling and Borrower's obligation to fund the resulting timing difference — so the borrower cannot later claim surprise.
*Recommendation:* Reflect the retainage in the re-certified draw schedule and confirm Borrower's liquidity to fund the timing gap, including the interaction with the $500,000 liquidity covenant in §13.2 and the $150,000 TI/LC reserve replenishment obligation in §6.3(c).

**F-3. Substantial completion carries an Event of Default but no cure; the draft adds a limited force majeure extension.**
*Record basis:* Term Sheet §§8.3, 11.1(h), 11.2(b) (non-monetary cure expressly excludes nothing about completion but excludes SPE, transfer and insurance defaults).
*Analysis:* The Term Sheet makes failure to achieve substantial completion by June 15, 2026 an Event of Default and does not specify a cure period. A hard deadline with no relief for permit or certificate-of-occupancy delay is common but harsh, particularly where the façade scope requires Board of Architectural Review approval.
*Draft treatment:* §7.4 and §16.1(j) implement the Event of Default; §16.2(e) permits Lender, in its discretion and on Borrower's timely request, to extend the deadline by up to 60 days for delays beyond Borrower's control (casualty, governmental permit or certificate-of-occupancy delay, labor disputes) not caused by Borrower, Guarantor or the Contractor.
*Recommendation:* Confirm the extension mechanic. It is a lender-protective mechanism (discretionary, capped, conditioned) rather than a borrower entitlement, and it reduces the risk of a technical default arising from City processing times.

**F-4. Change order control and Contractor lien exposure.**
*Record basis:* Term Sheet §8.1 (Contractor; copy of executed contract and all amendments before closing); §8.4 (lien waivers; date-down endorsements); §6.4(i)–(iii).
*Analysis:* The Construction Contract is not in the file, so we cannot confirm its payment terms, retainage provisions, lien waiver obligations, completion dates or whether it contains a consent-to-assignment of contract rights in Lender's favor (Term Sheet §5.1(g) requires the assignment of Borrower's interest in the renovation contract).
*Draft treatment:* §7.6 caps Borrower's unilateral change order authority at $100,000 in the aggregate (the Term Sheet does not address change orders — this is a Lender-protective addition); §7.2(b)–(d) require conditional and unconditional lien waivers and a date-down endorsement; §7.10 requires permits and Board of Architectural Review approval.
*Recommendation:* Review the Construction Contract before closing for assignability, lien waiver mechanics, retainage, and completion schedule compatibility with June 15, 2026; confirm the Contractor's payment and performance bonds (if any) and additional insured status.

**F-5. The renovation schedule assumes leases that the leasing projections do not support.**
*Record basis:* Renovation Budget and Draw Schedule (TI draws for Bay 2 from Month 6, October 2025, and for Suite B from Month 9, January 2026); Rent Roll, Vacancy Schedule tab (Bay 2 lease execution projected October 2025; Suite B marketing to begin July 2026 with lease execution November 2026 and rent commencement February 1, 2027).
*Analysis:* The draw schedule spends Suite B tenant improvement dollars from January 2026, six months after the marketing of Suite B is projected to begin (July 2026) and ten months before its projected lease execution (November 2026). Either the draw schedule is optimistic or the lease-up projections are not the plan of record. The difference matters because the Holdback is the funding source for those TI dollars and the DSCR test depends on Suite B being leased.
*Draft treatment:* §7.2(f) conditions TI-related draws on an executed, Lender-approved lease, which prevents a draw for an unleased space.
*Recommendation:* Ask Borrower to state which schedule is the plan of record, and re-certify both.

### G. Insurance

*Record basis:* Term Sheet §9.3; Phase I §2 (Zone X, Panel 45019C0520J effective December 4, 2020); Appraisal §2.1 (Zone X, "no mandatory flood insurance requirement under federal regulation"); §5 (same).

### H. Financial reporting and covenants

**H-1. The audited financial statement requirement conflicts with the Operating Agreement's reporting standard.**
*Record basis:* Term Sheet §7.3(a) (annual audited statements within 120 days); OA Summary §6.2 (annual statements "reviewed (but not audited)" by an independent CPA within 90 days).
*Analysis:* Borrower is a single-asset, single-purpose LLC whose Operating Agreement and member arrangements contemplate reviewed statements. If the loan documents require audited statements and the company's governing document and member agreements provide only reviewed, Borrower will be in default under §16.1(b) every year unless it voluntarily upgrades its audit standard at its own cost.
*Draft treatment:* §13.3(a) follows the Term Sheet and requires audited statements; §13.3(b) requires Guarantor's personal financial statement; §13.4 requires a compliance certificate.
*Recommendation:* Confirm whether Lender will accept annual reviewed statements (with an audit right on request) for a single-asset SPE. If audited statements are required, the requirement should be reflected in the Operating Agreement Amendment and priced into the borrower's closing costs. This is the sort of covenant that is harmless at closing and becomes an avoidable default at the first reporting date.

**H-2. The net worth and liquidity covenant is attributed to Borrower in the Term Sheet and to Guarantor in the markup notes.**
*Record basis:* Term Sheet §7.2 ("Borrower shall maintain at all times… net worth of not less than $1,000,000… liquid assets… not less than $500,000"); Prior Counsel Notes §6 ("Guarantor minimum net worth of not less than $1,000,000… Guarantor minimum liquid assets of not less than $500,000").
*Analysis:* We followed the Term Sheet (§13.2 applies the covenants to Borrower). If the intent was to impose them on Guarantor, the thresholds are not meaningful: Guarantor's stated net worth is $28,000,000. A $1,000,000 net worth floor for a guarantor of a $14,750,000 loan is a covenant in form only.
*Draft treatment:* §13.2 (Borrower), tested annually against the statements delivered under §13.3; the definition of liquid assets follows the Term Sheet (cash, cash equivalents, marketable securities, unencumbered deposits at federally insured institutions).
*Recommendation:* Confirm the intended obligor. If the covenant is meant to constrain Guarantor, we recommend a threshold consistent with a $14,750,000 guaranty (for example, net worth of at least $15,000,000 and liquid assets of at least $2,000,000), tested annually with a certificate.

**H-3. The DSCR test date is stated inconsistently in three documents.**
*Record basis:* Term Sheet §7.1 ("testing shall commence twenty-four (24) months after the date of closing, with the first test date to be the first full calendar quarter ending after the twenty-fourth month following closing (anticipated to be approximately July 15, 2027, for the quarter ending June 30, 2027)"); Prior Counsel Notes §6 ("beginning 24 months post-closing (first test date April 15, 2027)"); Rent Roll, Summary tab ("DSCR Covenant Testing Commencement: April 15, 2027 (Month 24 post-closing)").
*Analysis:* Closing on April 15, 2025 plus 24 months is April 15, 2027. The first full calendar quarter ending after that date is the quarter ending June 30, 2027; the Term Sheet's own parenthetical anticipates a test around July 15, 2027 for that quarter. The markup notes and the rent roll both say April 15, 2027, which is the end of the interest-only period, not the end of a calendar quarter. The Term Sheet is the executed instrument, so we followed it, but note a second, smaller inconsistency inside it: the phrase "first test date" and the parenthetical "approximately July 15, 2027" describe a determination date, while the test is measured as of the quarter ending June 30, 2027. There is a further timing point: quarterly rent rolls are due 30 days after quarter end (July 30, 2027), which is later than the July 15 date anticipated in the Term Sheet.
*Draft treatment:* §13.1(a) fixes the DSCR Test Date as the last day of each calendar quarter beginning with the quarter ending June 30, 2027; §13.4 ties the compliance certificate to the financial statement delivery dates; §13.5 gives Borrower 30 days after the compliance certificate due date to fund a cure deposit. The definition avoids reliance on a separate "test date" concept that could be read as a determination date.
*Recommendation:* Confirm the intended first test date with you and with the servicing group, and align the credit approval memo and the loan system to the loan documents. If the intent was April 15, 2027 (as the markup notes state), the draft must be changed, because the difference is one full quarter of covenant exposure immediately following the end of the interest-only period.

**H-4. Reporting obligations are otherwise consistent with the Term Sheet.**
*Record basis:* Term Sheet §7.3(a)–(e).
*Draft treatment:* §13.3(a)–(g) tracks the Term Sheet (audited financials within 120 days; Guarantor personal financial statement within 120 days of calendar year end; quarterly certified rent rolls within 30 days; annual operating statements with budget comparison within 120 days; leases and modifications within 10 business days) and adds a compliance certificate, a tax and insurance document covenant, and a catch-all information right.
*Recommendation:* None, other than Issue H-1.

### I. Transfer restrictions and change of control

**I-1. The "transfers among existing members" carve-out in the Term Sheet could permit a change of control without Lender consent.**
*Record basis:* Term Sheet §10.3 (no transfer of ownership interests exceeding 10% individually or 25% in the aggregate without consent, "except for transfers among the existing members of Borrower"); OA Summary §§4.1, 4.2, 4.3, 4.4.
*Analysis:* Read literally, the exception permits GDG to transfer its entire 72% interest to Tidewater or Harborline (a transfer "among the existing members") without Lender consent — converting the guarantor-controlled borrower into a fund-controlled borrower and defeating the non-recourse carve-out structure that depends on Graydon's incentives. The Operating Agreement does not fill the gap: Section 4.1 restricts transfers of membership interests but requires 75% approval calculated excluding the transferring member, Section 4.2(c) permits Tidewater to transfer to a "successor fund" without any consent, and Section 4.2 expressly does not address upstream changes in the ownership or control of any Member.
*Draft treatment:* §10.2(b)(iii) narrows the carve-out to transfers among existing Members that do not increase the GDG/Graydon aggregate interest above 72%, do not reduce GDG below 51%, do not result in any person other than GDG serving as Managing Member, and do not otherwise change control; §10.2(c) brings indirect and upstream changes within the consent requirement, including transfers of interests in GDG, replacement of Tidewater's general partner, and "successor fund" transfers; §10.2(e) makes a violation void ab initio and an Event of Default with no cure period (§16.1(k), §16.2(c)); §18.2(e) makes it a full-recourse carve-out.
*Recommendation:* **This is a deliberate narrowing of an executed commercial term and requires your approval.** The Term Sheet permits Lender to require additional provisions that are "not materially inconsistent" with its terms (§14.4); a transfer covenant that captures change of control is standard in non-recourse lending and, in our view, is consistent with the Term Sheet's evident purpose (protecting the Guarantor's control), but it is more restrictive than the literal carve-out and borrower's counsel will notice. Raise it with Marcus before the draft goes out.

**I-2. Upstream transfers are the real risk, not transfers of membership interests.**
*Record basis:* OA Summary §4.2 (illustrations: Mr. Graydon could sell his interest in GDG; Tidewater GP Holdings LLC could be acquired or replaced; Harborline's internal membership could change entirely — none of which would be a transfer of a membership interest in the Company); §4.5 (Affiliate definition).
*Analysis:* Because the SPE structure and the guaranty both depend on who controls GDG, an indirect change of control is functionally identical to a direct transfer of interests.
*Draft treatment:* §10.2(c) covers any change of control of a Controlling Member; §9.13(f) requires notice of any change in the identity of any Member, the Managing Member, the general partner of any Member, or any manager or officer of Borrower.
*Recommendation:* Require the Operating Agreement Amendment to add a parallel change-of-control restriction at the Member level — the Operating Agreement as delivered has none, and a loan-document-only restriction leaves the organizational documents silent (and potentially in conflict).

### E. Loan economics

**E-1. The DSCR covenant cannot be satisfied at any occupancy, on the borrower's own projections.**
*Record basis:* Term Sheet §§7.1 (1.25x minimum, testing from month 24), 11.1(i) (two consecutive quarters below 1.25x is an Event of Default); Rent Roll, Vacancy Schedule tab (stabilized best-case NOI $622,772; debt service $93,500 per month / $1,122,000 per year; DSCR 0.555x; "DOES NOT MEET 1.25x COVENANT"; realistic scenario NOI $314,782; DSCR 0.281x).
*Analysis:* We recomputed the debt service rather than adopting the workbook's figure: 25-year amortization of $14,750,000 at 5.85% produces $93,686.61 per month and $1,124,239 per year. Against best-case stabilized NOI of $622,772, that is a DSCR of **0.554x**; on an interest-only basis, $622,772 ÷ $862,875 = **0.722x**; on the workbook's "realistic" scenario, **0.280x**. The requirement of 1.25x on amortizing debt service implies required NOI of **$1,405,299**, or $45.33 per square foot across 31,000 square feet, against market rents of $24.00–$32.00 per square foot for ground-floor retail and $19.00–$25.00 per square foot for Class B office. Even with all 31,000 square feet leased at the rent roll's stabilized rents ($755,549 of gross revenue) and zero operating expenses, the DSCR would be 0.672x. There is no occupancy outcome that satisfies the covenant. This is not a lease-up timing risk; it is a structural mismatch between the loan amount, the debt service and the Property's income.
*Draft treatment:* §13.1 defines DSCR, Net Operating Income and Annual Debt Service with the specificity the Term Sheet leaves open (Term Sheet §7.1: "The precise definitions … shall be set forth in the Loan Documents"); Net Operating Income excludes non-recurring items, insurance and condemnation proceeds, capital expenditures and expenses funded from reserves, caps management fees at 4% of gross revenue, and Annual Debt Service is calculated on the 25-year amortization at the greater of the current rate and the floor rate. §13.1(d) grosses up debt service to the full $14,750,000 even before full disbursement. §13.5 provides a cure-deposit mechanism (a deposit equal to the NOI shortfall divided by 0.125, released after two consecutive compliant test dates). §16.1(g) implements the Term Sheet's two-quarter default trigger.
*Recommendation:* This requires a credit decision, not a drafting decision. The options, in order of structural soundness: (i) reduce the loan amount or extend the interest-only period so that the covenant is achievable on stabilized NOI; (ii) replace the amortizing DSCR test with an interest-only DSCR test at a lower threshold (for example, 1.00x on interest-only debt service, which still implies required NOI of $862,875 — itself 39% above the best-case projection); (iii) retain the covenant but require a funded debt service reserve equal to 12 months of debt service plus an extended interest-shortfall guaranty running beyond the first test date; (iv) require a cash sweep at any DSCR below 1.10x with a hard lockbox. As drafted, the Loan will be in default by the second test date absent one of these changes, and a covenant that the lender knows will be breached is worse than no covenant — it invites a waiver practice and, in a bankruptcy, an argument that the lender never expected compliance.
